title: Whether You Eat or Drink: The Verse You Thought Was Simple but Changes Everything
paragraphs:
Whether You Eat or Drink: The Verse You Thought Was Simple but Changes Everything
The Deeper Meaning of 1 Corinthians 10:31 and Why Jesus Never Intended Your Faith to Stay Inside a Church Building
Most people think their biggest spiritual moments happen in church.

A worship song.
A powerful sermon.
A tear-filled prayer at an altar.
But Scripture quietly destroys that assumption with one sentence.
One sentence so simple that many believers read past it without realizing it may be one of the most life-altering commands in the entire New Testament.
The Apostle Paul writes:
— 1 Corinthians 10:31 (KJV)
In the original Greek text, Paul wrote:

Εἴτε οὖν ἐσθίετε εἴτε πίνετε εἴτε τι ποιεῖτε, πάντα εἰς δόξαν Θεοῦ ποιεῖτε
(Eite oun esthiete eite pinete eite ti poieite, panta eis doxan Theou poieite)
Literally:
“Whether you eat, whether you drink, whether anything you do, do everything unto the glory of God.”
Everything.
Not some things.
Not only spiritual things.
Not only church things.
Everything.
The Greek word πάντα (panta) means “all things,” “everything,” “without exception.”
Paul intentionally chose the broadest possible word.
Because God was never interested in being merely part of your life.
He intended to be the reason for your entire life.
And that changes everything.
The shocking reality is that many people spend years trying to discover God's purpose while overlooking the purpose already sitting in front of them.
We ask:
“What is God's will for my life?”
Yet Scripture repeatedly answers:
“Glorify Him.”
Before God reveals where He wants you to go, He teaches you why you exist.
The Westminster Shorter Catechism famously summarized biblical truth:
“The chief end of man is to glorify God and enjoy Him forever.”
That is not merely theology.
That is reality.
You were created for His glory.
Isaiah 43:7 declares:
“Everyone who is called by my name, whom I created for my glory.”
The Hebrew word for glory is:
כָּבוֹד (kavod)
Originally carrying the idea of weight, substance, significance, and worth.
God's glory is His infinite worth displayed.
To glorify God means to make His worth visible.
It means living in a way that causes people to see that Jesus is valuable.
Suddenly 1 Corinthians 10:31 becomes much bigger than table manners.
Paul was addressing believers wrestling with difficult cultural issues involving food sacrificed to idols.
The Corinthians wanted a list of rules.
Instead, Paul gave them a greater principle.
Not:
“Can I do this?”
But:
“Does this glorify God?”
Not:
“Is it technically allowed?”
But:
“Will Christ be honored?”
Many believers today still ask the wrong question.
“How close can I get to sin without crossing the line?”
“How much compromise can I afford?”
“How much worldliness can I keep?”
Those questions reveal a heart looking for loopholes.
Love does not search for loopholes.
Love searches for opportunities to honor the One it loves.
The deeper issue was never food.
The deeper issue was worship.
And worship is far bigger than singing.
The Greek word often translated worship in Scripture is connected to the concept of devotion, reverence, and complete surrender.
Worship is not merely something you attend.
Worship is something you become.
The greatest act of worship may happen nowhere near a church stage.
It may happen in a hospital room.
A factory floor.
A classroom.
A kitchen.
A prison cell.
A lonely apartment.
A difficult marriage.
A painful season nobody else sees.
The real test of worship is not what happens when music starts.
The real test is what happens when life hurts.
Can Christ still be glorified there?
Many people assume God's glory shines brightest through perfect people.
The Bible repeatedly proves the opposite.
Abraham lied.
Jacob deceived.
Moses killed.
David committed adultery.
Peter denied Christ.
Paul persecuted believers.
Yet God transformed their stories.
Because the Gospel has always been about something greater than human perfection.
It has always been about divine redemption.
This is why our theme matters so deeply:
The entire Bible is filled with people who should have been disqualified.
People whose failures became headlines.
People who carried shame like chains.
People who thought their story was over.
Then Jesus stepped in.
The woman caught in adultery thought her scandal would define her.
Instead, grace rewrote her future.
Peter thought his denial ended everything.
Grace restored him.
Paul thought Christians were enemies.
Grace turned him into an apostle.
The cross itself looked like history's greatest scandal.
Yet God transformed it into history's greatest victory.
That is what grace does.
It rewrites.
Maybe that is why this verse strikes so deeply.
Because glorifying God is not about pretending to be flawless.
It is about allowing Christ to display His power through your surrendered life.
Even your scars.
Even your failures.
Even your darkest chapters.
Especially those.
The world knows how to celebrate success.
Only the Gospel knows how to redeem failure.
When people see Jesus transforming a broken life, they see glory.
When they see forgiveness replacing bitterness, they see glory.
When they see faith surviving suffering, they see glory.
When they see grace triumphing over scandal, they see glory.
And perhaps that is where this verse becomes intensely personal.
Because every reader eventually faces the same question.
What is your life pointing toward?
Your conversations.
Your social media.
Your relationships.
Your ambitions.
Your spending.
Your entertainment.
Your private thoughts.
Your hidden struggles.
Your victories.
Your wounds.
Your entire story.
Does it point people toward you?
Or toward Jesus?
One day every achievement will fade.
Every trophy will gather dust.
Every earthly accomplishment will become history.
But the glory given to Christ will echo into eternity.
That is why Paul says:
“Whatever you do.”
Because every ordinary moment becomes sacred when offered to God.
Every meal.
Every conversation.
Every decision.
Every act of kindness.
Every sacrifice.
Every unseen act of obedience.
Every step of faith.
All of it matters.
All of it can glorify Him.
And all of it can become part of a story Jesus is still rewriting.
Maybe you came here carrying regret.
Maybe there are chapters of your life you wish nobody knew.
Maybe you feel defined by mistakes that still haunt you.
Read this carefully:
Jesus is not intimidated by your scandal.
He specializes in rewriting impossible stories.
The same grace that transformed Peter, Paul, David, and countless others is still transforming people today.
Your worst chapter does not have to be your final chapter.
The Author is still writing.
And His pen has always been dipped in grace.
If this message stirred something inside you, don't keep it to yourself.
What part of your story are you trusting Jesus to rewrite?
“I believe grace is still writing my story.”
Your testimony may become someone else's reason to keep going.

If your desire is truly to glorify God, one practical way to participate is by helping spread biblical truth through sharing, supporting, and partnering with ministries that faithfully proclaim Jesus Christ.
Because the greatest tragedy is not having a broken past.
The greatest tragedy is believing Jesus cannot redeem it.
